newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian investors await earnings recovery.
newsitem.headline: Australian investors await earnings recovery.

text.p: A lacklustre performance by Australian shares on Thursday despite a 96 point rise by the Dow Jones Industrial Average and a local interest rate cut on Wednesday underscores the mediocre outlook for Australian corporate earnings and the stock market itself, analysts said.

"People have been waiting for company profits to be a lot healthier than they have been," said Marcus Tuck, economist at broker James Capel. "Trading statements coming from companies have been pretty cautious on that front," he said.
The All Ordinaries index closed 13.9 points lower at 2,346.7 on Thursday as the market ignored the Dow's post-election jump and a 0.5 percent cut in official interest rates on Wednesday.

"What we have been pointing out is that the economy appears to be a little bit softer -- there is probably the risk of more earnings downgrades in the short term," said John Banos, equity strategist at McIntosh Securities.
Banos said McIntosh's 12 month forecast for the index was 2,300 and the broker believed the negative trend for Australian company earnings would last for another quarter.
Nowhere are earnings jitters more evident than in the core mining and metals industries.
Metals recycler Simsmetal Ltd started a trend last month, reporting a 34 percent fall in first quarter profit.
"People have been waiting for higher commodity prices to come through for some time now and there is still a lingering concern," Capel's Tuck said.
Major mining houses have recently followed the trend by warning weak base metal prices coupled with a strong Australian dollar would likely depress earnings this financial year.
At it annual meeting last month, MIM Holdings Ltd was cautious. "Given the present level of copper prices in particular, a difficult year is in prospect," MIM said.

Mining and forestry group North Ltd was even less optimistic at its annual meeting on October 31. "The current indications are that the 1996/7 (year) will be a flat trading year with results being affected by subdued prospects for prices for most of our commodities," chairman Micheal Deeley said.
One of the most worrying signals for the market has come its largest company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd.
BHP's earnings uncertainty emerged at the start of September when managing director John Prescott told Reuters that trading conditions in the world steel market could be deteriorating.

Later that month Prescott said that if copper prices did not improve, it would be a challenge for BHP to overcome. BHP reported a 23 percent fall in net profit to A$287 million for its first quarter ending August 31, as a strong Australian dollar exacerbated the impact of weak copper and steel markets.
"A lot of the commodity price forecasts that are underlying earnings forecasts to our mind are a still little bit high," said Phillip Graham, economist at broker ANZ MacCaughan.
"In some cases they are assuming half year averages which are virtually impossible to get," Graham said.
Graham said this would mean profit forecasts for many resource companies were likely to be revised downwards.
ANZ McCaughan forecasts the All Ordinaries index to be at 2350 by December 31.
"The only companies to have pretty healthy earnings are industrial companies with exposure to the services sectors like banks, insurers and gamblers," Tuck said.
Tuck said this trend was likely to continue.
"The interest rate sensitive services will be the ones to continue to do best until such time that cyclical recovery in the economy looks more firmly based," he said.
Tuck expects the index to be at 2400 by the end of 1996.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
